ON BEHALF OF FLEMING SPRINGS RANCH PAGE 2

 I. INTRODUCTION

Q: Please state your name and relationship to this proceeding.

A: My name is Dawn Laurel - Jones, and I am associated with The Fleming Springs Ranch Land
Company LLC, owner of the Fleming Springs Ranch. I am testifying on behalf of the Fleming
Springs Ranch.

Q: Have you ever testified in a Public Utility Commission of Texas (“PUC”) proceeding?
A. No.

Q: Is Fleming Springs Ranch Land Company LLC, an affected landowner in this Case?
A: Yes. The Fleming Springs Ranch Land Company LLC owns the Fleming Springs Ranch
consisting of approximately 5,700 acres located in San Saba County. Ranch property would be
affected by Link U5 and additional ranch property and springs would be affected by Link U6.

Q: Are you familiar with the area in which applicants propose to install the transmission
line?
A: Yes.

I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF TESTIMONY

Q: What is the purpose of your testimony?

A: The purpose of my testimony is to confirm that the Fleming Springs Ranch Land Company
LLC, that owns the Fleming Springs Ranch, opposes the selection of any route that would include
Link U5 and U6 which could cause serious harm to the proposed routes crossing the Fleming
Springs Ranch, its neighbors ranches and farms, San Saba municipal water, ecological sites,
wildlife sites, indigenous sites, historical sites, and the scenic byways that have attracted a growth

in tourism and economic benefit for the community of San Saba.

Tf. DESCRIPTION OF PROPERTY AND THE LINE'S IMPACT
Q: Where is your property located?
A: The Fleming Springs Ranch is located 4-5 miles East of the town of San Saba on the south side
of HWY 190. Exhibit 1 below provides a map of the ranch’s location and identifies certain

structures and improvements on and near the ranch:

Q: In general, what are your routing concerns?

A: The Commission should not approve a route that includes Link US and Link U6. These links
would affect the Fleming Springs Ranch, its wildlife and livestock, its neighbors, the community
of San Saba, municipal water the community greatly depends on, Simpson Creek, Fleming Springs
Branch, Barnett Springs Creek feeding the San Saba and Colorado Rivers. Any route that includes
Link US and U6 would require construction through deep canyon lands with unstable limestone
soils, high-density archaeological zones, aquifer/spring recharge and discharge features, and steep
slope areas requiring extensive access road construction. The proposed U5 and U6 structures
would also shadow the historic county seat community, and impede the few roads in and around
the community and its landowners during construction. It would impact indigenous sites like 5
Mile Hill, which is partially located on the Fleming Springs Ranch south of HWY 190 and was
used by the Comanche to signal other tribal sites in other distant locations. It would also impact

historical homestead sites located on Simpson Creek near HWY 190 established by Captain John
W. Barmett, veteran of the Mexican War who was a founder of San Saba, permanently degrade
scenic views of the Fleming Springs Ranch, including its neighbors, and negatively affect existing

eco/nature tourism and its growth that has helped boost a depressed economy.

Q: What detrimental impact does Link U5 and U6 have upon the Fleming Springs Ranch?

A: The construction and permanent presence of a 765-kV. transmission line links US and U6 along
this corridor would have a negative impact on the value of years of careful prairie restoration for
wildlife and livestock on water distribution, harm to surrounding wildlife habitats, archeological

sites, and diminish the overall aesthetics.

Q: Please describe the landscape of the Fleming Springs Ranch.

A: The Fleming Springs Ranch includes frontage on the Fleming Springs Branch along its northern
boundary and is defined by the canyon system and its many tributaries, which cut through the
property from the uplands down to the San Saba River and ultimately the Colorado River. The
landscape is characterized by the rugged karst topography and deep canyon cuts through limestone,
steep high-angle slopes, rocky outcrops, caves, sinkholes, and fractures through the surface rock.

The property contains numerous freshwater springs located within the canyon riparian bottoms.

Q: Are there any cultural and archaeological resources on the property?

A: The Lower Colorado River is internationally recognized for its unparalleled archeological
resources, including habitation shelters, and deeply stratified cultural deposits. Any route through
or near this corridor, including access roads, staging areas, or vegetation clearing, would risk

irreparable harm to these resources.

The main house of the Fleming Springs Ranch is located on top of the Fleming Springs Branch,
commissioned by Jeremiah Fleming in 1856, built by Bavarian Stone Masons with Ellenburger
outcropping limestone, a stones throw from the house. Native American artifacts have been found
in the spring, and around the house, including from the Fleming Springs Ranch house spring fed

pool, down the Fleming Branch, and Simpson Creek to the San Saba River. These artifacts are

Q: Describe the wildlife and ecological resources at the Fleming Springs Ranch

A: The Fleming Springs Ranch, located on the northern edge of the Edwards Plateau includes
terrain consisting of rocky limestone hills, Ashe juniper/oak woodlands, and savanna areas. San
Saba, known as the "Pecan Capital of the World," features a rich riparian ecosystem along the
Fleming Springs Branch, Simpson Creek, and Barnett Springs Creek, and various other aquifer

recharge zones characterized by limestone hills, pecan woodlands, and diverse wildlife. We have

preserved over 16 varieties of Oaks along with large mesquite and old growth Ashe Juniper as
canopy for wildlife and livestock. The ranch has serval varieties of pecan trees including Native
Texas Pecans on or near the Fleming Springs Branch. The ranch supports Little Bluestem, Texas

Cup Grass, Sideoats Grama, Big Bluestem, and Buffalo Grass.

The area is crucial for white-tailed deer, migratory birds, and native game species.

The Fleming Springs Ranch wildlife includes white-tailed deer, wild turkey, Bob White quail,
coyotes, bobcats, cougars, Texas rat snakes, Western Diamondback rattlesnakes, Redstripe Ribbon
Snakes, and various other small mammals. The Aves include White-eyed Vireos, Yellow-Throated
Vireos, Kingfishers, Canyon Wrens, Summer Tanagers, Eastern screech owls, Chimney Swifts,
Ravens, Turkey Vultures, Black Vultures, and various raptors. Migratory birds include Painted
Buntings, Grey Catbird, Yellow-billed Cuckoos, Vermillion Flycatchers, Scissor tailed
Flycatchers, Orchard Oriole and Black Bellied Whistling Ducks. The Fleming Springs Ranch
offers stop over habitat throughout our riparian areas along our springs, water run off, and aquifer
recharge zones. The native insects of the area aid pollination and function as a food source to help
provide key habitats for birding and ecological viewing. These habitat provide essential food and

rest for birds migrating through the Central Flyway.

Part of the Fleming Springs Ranch is high fenced. The Fleming Springs Ranch commercial deer
lease program works closely with the Texas Parks and Wildlife to prevent degradation of natural
habitats to protect biodiversity. We have successfully cultivated robust and healthy native white
tail deer through our dedicated habitat preservation efforts. Exhibit 4, 5, 6 & 7 below provide
evidence of the quality of native white tail deer, maintenance of springs, financial investment, and
years of work. We volunteer to restore and conserve these habitats by protecting river banks,
planting native grasses throughout the ranch, clearing invasive species, and preserving old growth
oaks, mesquite, and juniper. We conduct multiple surveys of our deer population for proper culling
data from the TPW. We provide the TPW our harvesting data along with any habitat preservation
managing non-native invasive plants such as Woolly Distaff Thistle, Cat Claw, and managing
predators like coyotes, and non-native invasive wildlife such as feral hogs who predate on juvenile

domestic livestock, white tail deer fawns ground nesting, bird nests, and various species of reptiles

Q: Do you have any concerns about the Transmission Line’s impact on the wildlife at the
Fleming Springs Ranch?

A: Yes. Building a 765kV transmission line on or next to the Fleming Springs Ranch would create
ongoing disturbance within a migration corridor that is currently open canyon and savannah habitat
for all variety of wildlife listed above. The 200’-250’ Links U5 and U6 proposed corridor routes
would fragment habitats, create migration barriers, increase collision risks for birds, increase
invasive species spread, and introduce noise, light, and electromagnetic force pollution. In

addition, there is already a preexisting 65’ high power line on and near the Fleming Springs Ranch.

Q: Describe the existing 65’ power line across the Fleming Springs Ranch

A: The 65’ transmission line runs across the Fleming Springs Ranch and our neighbors south of
HWY 190 near 5 Mile Hill and travels West to and through an existing LCRA power station on
HWY 190 and Texas Park Road 400. This power line already diminishes the scenic views on the
Fleming Springs Ranch, but also causes potential risks when managing the growing feral hog
population via helicopter three times a year on our ranch, and over our neighbors to reduce the
inevitable damage to properties and the constant threat to our county’s biodiversity. 765-kV
transmission line links U5 and U6 would add further risks to our land management efforts, and
dwarf the existing power lines. The sheer size of 765 kV lines would definitely diminish the scenic
views from the Fleming Springs Ranch and the community of San Saba. Exhibit 8 & 9 below
proved evidence of the pre-existing power line on the Fleming Springs Ranch facing north toward
HWY 190, and how much higher the 765-kV towers would be as compared to the pre-existing

lines.

Q: Describe the hydrological resources around your property?

A: The Fleming Springs ranch has a variety of hydrological resources across the ranch that include
the Fleming Springs Branch, Simpson Creek, and Barnett Creek which are all part of the
Ellenburger-San Saba and Marble Falls Aquifer. The Ellenburger-San Saba is a minor aquifer that
is found in parts of 16 counties in the Llano Uplift area of Central Texas. The aquifer consists of
the Tanyard, Gorman, and Honeycut formations of the Ellenburger Group and the San Saba
Limestone Member of the Wilberns Formation. The aquifer consists of a sequence of limestone
and dolomite that crop out in a circular pattern around the Llano Uplift and dip radially into the
subsurface away from the center of the uplift to depths of approximately 3,000 feet. Regional block
faulting has significantly compartmentalized the aquifer. The maximum thickness of the aquifer is

about 2,700 feet. Water occurs in fractures, cavities, and solution channels and is commonly under

confined conditions. The aquifer is highly permeable in places, as indicated by wells that yield as
much as 1,000 gallons per minute. Numerous springs issue from the aquifer, maintaining the
baseflow of streams in the area. Groundwater in the Ellenburger-San Saba Aquifer is generally
very good and usually has less than 1,000 milligrams per liter of total dissolved solids. Total
dissolved solids increase down-dip and radially outward from the Llano Uplift, centered in Llano
County. Elevated concentrations of radionuclides also occur in the aquifer, mostly in the northern
part of the aquifer. Most of the groundwater the Fleming Springs ranch uses is for used for is
irrigation and livestock. A smaller portion is used for the two residences and guest quarters on

the ranch.

A large portion of water flowing from San Saba Springs, which is the water supply for the city of
San Saba, is thought to be from the Ellenburger-San Saba and Marble Falls aquifers. Springs in
this region contribute essential baseflow to the San Saba River and ultimately to the Colorado
River, supporting agriculture, municipal water for the San Saba community, and riparian and
estuarine habitat systems. The Fleming Springs Ranch contains three important springs previously
listed, and is influenced by diffuse recharge zones, karst features or sink depressions and spring

discharge areas.

If Links U5 and U6 cross these aquifer recharge zones described above, including Simpson Creek,
Fleming Springs Branch, and Barnett Creek, the infrastructure disturbances in these areas risk
compromising flow quantity and quality, potentially affecting these and other riparian creeks and
streams that may harm the entire community of the city of San Saba and it’s greater population

which is historically dependent on these water resources.

A: Do not use Links U5 and U6.

Q: Does this conclude your direct case testimony?

A. Yes. Thank you for your consideration on this very important matter.
